map.Ban all employment for teenagers of ever: Limit how much employers can pay workers under eighteen
map.Require teenagers to work after school e: Make schools provide job training to teenage students

ww.Limit how much employers can pay workers: Child labor law restricts hours and hazardous tasks for minors, not their pay rates; wages for young workers fall under the minimum wage rules instead.
ww.Make schools provide job training to tee: Child labor law limits when and how minors may work; it does not set up school job training, and no teenager is required to take a job.

map.Unlimited hours at any time of day or ni: Up to forty hours a week during the school year
map.They are not allowed to work at all in a: Full-time work is allowed after ninth grade

ww.Up to forty hours a week during the scho: Federal rules cap work for 14- and 15-year-olds at about 18 hours in a school week, so forty hours a week during school is far too many.
ww.Full-time work is allowed after ninth gr: Federal hour limits for 14- and 15-year-olds depend on age, not grade level, so finishing ninth grade does not unlock full-time work.

map.Only after two denials: One free report per two-year period
map.Never; each costs money: After paying a monthly membership fee

ww.One free report per two-year period: Federal law gives each consumer a free report from each bureau at least once a year, so a two-year wait between free reports is longer than required.
ww.Twice during a lifetime: Consumers are not limited to two free reports in a lifetime; the law allows a free copy from each bureau at least once every twelve months.
ww.After paying a monthly membership fee: A free annual report requires no membership or fee; consumers can get it from annualcreditreport.com at no charge, so a paid subscription is not needed.

map.A tax paid only by wealthy individuals e: A fee that creditors pay to collect old debts
map.A method of avoiding every kind of tax o: A payment plan offered by banks to new borrowers

ww.A fee that creditors pay to collect old: Bankruptcy is a court proceeding filed by a debtor who cannot repay; creditors do not pay a fee to collect, and it is not a charge of any sort.
ww.A payment plan offered by banks to new b: Bankruptcy is a court process, not a bank product; banks do not offer it, and it exists for debtors who cannot meet their obligations.

map.Prevents the debtor from filing any taxe: Requires the debtor to repay creditors within thirty days
map.Cancels all of the debtor's debts instan: Permanently erases the debtor's debts once a petition is filed

ww.Requires the debtor to repay creditors w: The stay pauses collection and gives the debtor breathing room; it does not set a thirty day repayment deadline, which would work against the protection.
ww.Permanently erases the debtor's debts on: Debts are not erased when a petition is filed; the stay is only a temporary pause, and a later discharge order is what eliminates eligible debts.

map.Bans every kind of closing fee at all: Caps the interest rate on home mortgage loans
map.Guarantees that a buyer gets a mortgage: Requires lenders to approve buyers with steady jobs

ww.Caps the interest rate on home mortgage: RESPA is about disclosure and kickbacks in settlement services; it does not cap mortgage interest rates, which depend on the lender and the market.
ww.Requires lenders to approve buyers with: RESPA does not tell lenders whom to approve; lenders decide on credit, income and other factors, and RESPA only requires them to disclose costs.

map.Free stock for every employee of the fir: Limits on what executives can earn in salary

ww.Regular dividends paid to investors: Sarbanes-Oxley does not require any dividend; the board decides whether to pay dividends, while the Act deals with internal controls and accurate financial reports.
ww.Limits on what executives can earn in sa: The Act does not cap executive pay; it requires certified financial statements and internal controls, and it created oversight for auditors.

map.A group that has no members and no asset: A company that pays taxes at a reduced rate
map.A business that never files forms with t: A firm that gets a refund on sales taxes paid

ww.A company that pays taxes at a reduced r: A tax-exempt organization is relieved of certain taxes rather than taxed at a lower rate, and its status comes from a charitable or similar purpose.
ww.A firm that gets a refund on sales taxes: Tax-exempt status relates to income tax for groups with a qualifying purpose; it is not a refund program for sales taxes paid by a business.

map.Sharing only good news with the public: Keeping decisions private until they are final
map.Hiding information from the public alway: Keeping results secret to protect the brand

ww.Keeping decisions private until they are: Transparency means openness about decisions as they are made and results afterward; keeping decisions private until they are final limits what stakeholders can see and judge.
ww.Keeping results secret to protect the br: Secrecy to protect a brand is the opposite of transparency, which asks a business to share results openly so people can trust it.

map.Only employees matter to the business: A company should focus on its workers' demands
map.Only the government matters in the end: A company should follow government priorities
map.Only shareholders matter, as they own it: A company should maximize profit for its owners

ww.A company should focus on its workers' d: Stakeholder theory weighs workers along with customers, suppliers, owners and communities; focusing on one group leaves out others the company affects.
ww.A company should follow government prior: Government is one stakeholder, and stakeholder theory asks managers to balance many groups rather than follow the priorities of a single one.
ww.A company should maximize profit for its: Maximizing owner profit is the shareholder view; stakeholder theory instead asks a company to weigh the interests of all groups affected.

map.Only the government and its agencies: Agencies that write the rules for an industry
map.Only the owners, since none else cares: Owners who put money into the business

ww.Agencies that write the rules for an ind: Regulators are one group with an interest, but the term stakeholders is much broader and covers anyone affected by what the business does.
ww.Owners who put money into the business: Owners are stakeholders, but the term also covers employees, customers, suppliers and communities, so owners alone are too narrow a definition.
ww.Firms that sell competing products: Competitors can be affected by a business, yet the term stakeholders covers every group with an interest, so rivals are only a small part of it.

map.Sets tariffs on imports for every countr: Sets tariff rates for goods moving between member nations
map.Regulates the stock markets of every mem: Funds development projects like dams and roads

ww.Sets tariff rates for goods moving betwe: Each nation sets its own tariffs, and the WTO handles trade rules; the IMF focuses on monetary cooperation and lending to countries in financial trouble.
ww.Funds development projects like dams and: Funding long-term development projects is the work of the World Bank, while the IMF deals with exchange rates and balance of payments problems.

map.Only foreign goods can use the label, no: Products must be designed by a U.S. company, wherever made
map.The label is always optional and false c: Labels are voluntary and false claims bring no penalty

ww.Products must be designed by a U.S. comp: The FTC standard looks at where the product is made, not where it was designed or who owns the company, so design alone does not support the claim.
ww.Labels are voluntary and false claims br: Using the label is voluntary, but a false Made in USA claim is a deceptive practice that the FTC can penalize.

map.A contract made by one person with no ot: A contract that one party may cancel at will
map.A contract that is made orally only, wit: A contract that must be signed in front of a notary

ww.A contract that one party may cancel at: Unilateral describes who makes a promise, not who can cancel; a contract that may be dropped at will may lack a binding promise altogether.
ww.A contract that must be signed in front: Notarization is not what makes a contract unilateral; the term refers to one party promising and the other accepting by performing.

map.Minors cannot own property or goods of t: Contracts with minors require a parent's signature to exist
map.The contract is void for every party who: The contract is binding once a minor turns sixteen

ww.Contracts with minors require a parent's: A parent's signature is not required for a minor's contract to exist; the contract is simply voidable by the minor, who can choose to cancel it.
ww.The contract is binding once a minor tur: The age of majority is generally eighteen, so turning sixteen does not make a minor's contract binding or take away the right to cancel.

map.The contract lasts forever and can never: The contract renews automatically each year until someone cancels it
map.Deadlines are optional and late work is: Deadlines are treated as targets and small delays are excused

ww.The contract renews automatically each y: Automatic renewal is a separate term about duration; time is of the essence concerns how strictly deadlines must be met, not how long the contract lasts.
ww.Deadlines are treated as targets and sma: The clause makes deadlines strict, so even a small delay can be a breach; treating dates as loose targets is the reverse of its purpose.

ww.Partner B must ratify it: Ratification by Partner B is not needed, because Partner A acted within the ordinary course of business as an agent and already bound the partnership.
ww.The contract is void: A contract made within the ordinary course of business is valid and enforceable against the partnership, so it is not void because Partner B was not told.
ww.The contract needs a vote: A partner acting in the ordinary course of business does not need a vote of the partners to bind the firm, so no vote is needed here.

map.No authority at all to act for anyone in: When an agent holds authority that the principal expressly gave in writing
map.Authority written in a contract only, ne: When an agent gains authority because the principal later approves the act

ww.When an agent holds authority that the p: That describes express authority, which is stated directly; apparent authority arises from the principal's conduct that leads a third party to believe the agent has authority.
ww.When an agent gains authority because th: That describes ratification, where the principal approves an act after it happens; apparent authority comes from the principal's conduct before the third party relied on it.

ww.The customer who ordered it: The customer who ordered the delivery did not cause the crash or control the driver, so liability falls on the driver and the employer.
ww.The customer's insurance company: The customer's insurer has no connection to the driver's negligence; liability falls on the driver and the employer under agency law.
ww.The driver's family members: A driver's relatives are not liable for the driver's torts on the job; responsibility rests with the driver and the employer under respondeat superior.

ww.Free city services: The Takings Clause requires fair payment for the land, not free services; the owner is entitled to just compensation, usually measured as market value.
ww.A property tax cut: A reduction in future property taxes does not replace payment for the land taken; the Fifth Amendment requires just compensation to the owner.

map.It must promise services only, never mon: It must be a signed writing that promises to deliver goods or services on a date
map.It must be spoken aloud before two witne: It must be notarized and filed with the county clerk before anyone can use it

ww.It must be a signed writing that promise: A negotiable instrument must promise payment of money, not delivery of goods or services; a signed writing that promises other performance does not qualify under Article 3.
ww.It must be notarized and filed with the: Neither notarization nor filing with a clerk is required for a negotiable instrument; Article 3 requires a signed writing with an unconditional promise to pay.

map.Only managers may speak about pay with o: Pay talk can be treated as disclosing trade secrets
map.Employees may never discuss pay, since w: Pay discussions need written permission from human resources
map.Pay is always secret by law in every sta: Wage data is confidential under federal privacy law

ww.Pay talk can be treated as disclosing tr: Wages are not trade secrets, and the National Labor Relations Act protects most employees who discuss pay, so such a rule may be unlawful.
ww.Pay discussions need written permission: Employees do not need permission to discuss wages with coworkers; the NLRA protects these talks, so requiring written permission may be unlawful.
ww.Wage data is confidential under federal: No federal privacy law makes wages confidential among coworkers; the NLRA protects pay discussions, so a blanket confidentiality rule can violate employee rights.

map.Chapter 7 is for businesses only, and Ch: Chapter 7 is for large corporations while Chapter 13 is for small ones
map.They are identical in every respect and: Chapter 7 covers family farms while Chapter 13 covers city governments

ww.Chapter 7 is for large corporations whil: Chapter 13 is only for individuals with regular income, and Chapter 7 is open to individuals as well; corporations reorganizing usually use Chapter 11.
ww.Chapter 7 covers family farms while Chap: Family farmers use Chapter 12 and municipalities use Chapter 9; Chapter 13 is a repayment plan for individuals with regular income.

map.A legal requirement for every product so: A government program that rewards firms for hiring workers locally
map.A sales tactic used only by the largest: An accounting method for reporting profit to shareholders each quarter

ww.A government program that rewards firms: Corporate social responsibility is a voluntary commitment by the company, not a government reward program for hiring; it covers broader social and environmental goals.
ww.An accounting method for reporting profi: Corporate social responsibility concerns ethical and social commitments, not accounting; profit reporting follows separate accounting standards and is not a form of responsibility.

map.Sue for the builder's profits only, in c: Ask the state to fine the builder instead of suing
map.Do nothing because no breach occurred ye: Do nothing, since a breach cannot happen before June

ww.Ask the state to fine the builder instea: A missed contract is a private civil matter, so the remedy is damages from the builder, not a state fine; the state does not penalize ordinary breach.
ww.Do nothing, since a breach cannot happen: A clear repudiation is a breach before the due date, so the homeowner need not wait for June and may act right away.

map.Doing exactly what was promised in every: Performance that misses the main purpose but is mostly finished
map.Doing none of the work that the contract: Payment made early so the other side must start the work

ww.Performance that misses the main purpose: Substantial performance requires meeting the essential purpose; work that misses the main purpose is a material breach, even if much of it is done.
ww.Payment made early so the other side mus: Early payment is a matter of timing and does not describe performance of the work; substantial performance means the work meets the contract's essential purpose.

map.A contract that is never signed by the p: A promise to pay a debt that was discharged in bankruptcy
map.A contract with no terms at all, written: A court remedy that cancels a contract because one side was misled by fraud

ww.A promise to pay a debt that was dischar: That describes reaffirmation of a discharged debt, not a substitute performance; an accord and satisfaction settles a dispute by accepting different performance.
ww.A court remedy that cancels a contract b: Cancellation for fraud is rescission, a remedy ordered by a court; an accord and satisfaction is an agreement between the parties themselves to substitute performance.

map.A gift that the company gives to every c: Void because the company gave no consideration
map.Always enforceable, since customers agre: Fully enforceable because the customer signed it

ww.Void because the company gave no conside: The company provides service in exchange for payment, so consideration exists; the fairness problem is the one-sided power to change terms without notice.
ww.Fully enforceable because the customer s: Courts can refuse to enforce unconscionable or illusory terms even when a customer signed, so a signature alone does not make every term enforceable.

map.A contract with no terms, only a blank p: A contract formed when a website visitor simply browses its pages
map.A contract written on paper only and sig: A contract that a buyer accepts by opening the box of software
map.A contract made only by phone, with no w: A contract that a lawyer drafts and e-mails to both sides for review

ww.A contract formed when a website visitor: That describes browsewrap, where no clear acceptance occurs; click-wrap requires the user to take an affirmative step, such as clicking I agree.
ww.A contract that a buyer accepts by openi: That describes shrink-wrap, where acceptance comes from opening packaging; click-wrap is an online agreement accepted by clicking a button.
ww.A contract that a lawyer drafts and e-ma: A negotiated, e-mailed draft is an ordinary written contract; click-wrap is a standard online form that the user accepts by clicking.

map.No, tablets are illegal for signing cont: No, E-SIGN covers e-mail contracts but not tablet signatures
map.No, only ink signatures count, so a type: No, a typed name must be followed by an ink signature
map.Only if notarized by a public notary and: Yes, if a witness signs the tablet screen too

ww.No, E-SIGN covers e-mail contracts but n: E-SIGN covers electronic signatures broadly, including those made on a tablet, so it does not exclude them from legal effect.
ww.No, a typed name must be followed by an: E-SIGN and UETA give a typed electronic signature the same effect as ink, so no follow-up handwritten signature is required for validity.
ww.Yes, if a witness signs the tablet scree: A witness is not required for an ordinary service contract; the signature is valid if the customer intended to sign electronically.

map.Never forms a contract between merchants: Is treated as a counteroffer that ends the original offer
map.Always replaces the original offer, what: Makes the added terms binding on the offeror right away

ww.Is treated as a counteroffer that ends t: That is the old mirror image rule; UCC 2-207 changed it so an acceptance with added terms can still form a contract for goods.
ww.Makes the added terms binding on the off: Added terms do not bind the offeror automatically; they are proposals that join the contract only if not material and not objected to.

map.Only after acceptance has been given and: Generally at any time until a month after the offer is made
map.Only by a court order after both sides h: Generally by a written notice filed with the court clerk
map.Never, because an offer once made must s: Generally not until the stated deadline has passed even without an option

ww.Generally at any time until a month afte: Revocation is not tied to a one month waiting period; an offeror may usually revoke at any time before acceptance unless an option or firm offer exists.
ww.Generally by a written notice filed with: Revocation is a private act communicated to the offeree; nothing needs to be filed with a court clerk for an offer to be withdrawn.
ww.Generally not until the stated deadline: Without an option or firm offer, an offeror may revoke before the deadline; a stated deadline alone does not bind the offeror to keep the offer open.

map.Always, since silence is a clear sign of: Often, since an offeree who says nothing is presumed to agree
map.Never, since silence has no effect on an: Usually, when the offeror mails the offer by certified mail
map.Only on weekends, when the offer is open: Typically, when the offer is made to a business instead of a consumer

ww.Often, since an offeree who says nothing: Silence is not normally acceptance, because an offeree has no duty to respond; acceptance by silence is limited to special situations such as prior dealings.
ww.Usually, when the offeror mails the offe: The mailing method of an offer does not turn silence into acceptance; the exceptions depend on prior dealings, accepted benefits or the parties' agreed terms.
ww.Typically, when the offer is made to a b: Silence is not usually acceptance for business offerees either; the exceptions turn on course of dealing or accepted benefits, not on whether the offeree is a business.

map.A seller may deliver any goods at all, w: A buyer must keep goods if the defect is cheap to fix
map.A seller may never deliver late, whateve: A seller must replace defective goods within thirty days of delivery date

ww.A buyer must keep goods if the defect is: Under the perfect tender rule, a buyer may reject goods that fail to conform even when the defect is cheap to fix, though the seller may get a chance to cure.
ww.A seller must replace defective goods wi: The UCC does not set a thirty day replacement rule; the perfect tender rule lets a buyer reject nonconforming goods, with a possible right of the seller to cure.

map.A limited warranty has no terms and give: A full warranty is sold for an added fee, while a limited warranty comes with the product
map.They are identical in every way and give: A full warranty must be in writing, while a limited warranty may be given orally
map.A full warranty lasts only one day, whil: A full warranty covers parts and labor for ten years, while a limited one covers one year

ww.A full warranty is sold for an added fee: Magnuson-Moss does not tie full warranties to a separate fee; a full warranty is a standard of coverage that a seller chooses to give with the product.
ww.A full warranty must be in writing, whil: Both full and limited written warranties are covered by the Act and must be written; the difference is the strength of the remedies, not the form.
ww.A full warranty covers parts and labor f: The labels full and limited describe the strength of remedies, not set durations; a full warranty need not last ten years, nor a limited one a single year.

map.A business owned by one person who also: A business owned by shareholders who buy stock on an open exchange
map.A business with no members that is run o: A business owned by partners who share personal liability

ww.A business owned by shareholders who buy: That describes a publicly traded corporation, where owners hold shares for investment; a cooperative is run by members who also use its services.
ww.A business owned by partners who share p: That describes a general partnership, where partners own the firm and are personally liable; a cooperative is democratically controlled by members who use its services.

map.No duties at all owed to the principal: Equal pay, safe conditions and training

ww.Equal pay, safe conditions and training: Pay, safe conditions and training are duties an employer may owe a worker; the agent owes the principal loyalty, obedience, care and accounting.
ww.Profit sharing and written notice: Agents do not owe profit sharing to the principal, and notice is not their main duty; their fiduciary duties are loyalty, obedience, care and accounting.

map.Only by a tax filing made with the reven: By a filing with the state agency that registers agents
map.Only by lawsuit brought in a court of la: By a judge's order after both sides have attended mediation
map.It can never end once it begins, whateve: By a change in the agent's home address or phone number

ww.By a filing with the state agency that r: Most agencies are not registered with the state, and no filing is needed to end one; it ends by agreement, completion, revocation or a party's death.
ww.By a judge's order after both sides have: Court orders and mediation are not required to end an agency; either party can usually end it by notice, and completion or death also ends it.
ww.By a change in the agent's home address: An address or phone change has no effect on the relationship; an agency ends by agreement, completion, revocation, renunciation or a party's death.

map.Liable only for tickets and parking fine: Yes, because the employee was on the company payroll that day
map.Liable only if the car is red, whatever: Yes, because employers must cover damages from personal trips
map.Always liable for everything the employe: No, because crashes are criminal matters, not civil ones

ww.Yes, because the employee was on the com: Being on the payroll does not make an employer liable for every act; liability depends on whether the employee was acting within the scope of employment.
ww.Yes, because employers must cover damage: No rule makes employers cover damages from personal trips; respondeat superior applies to acts within the scope of employment.
ww.No, because crashes are criminal matters: Crashes can lead to civil liability as well as criminal charges; the employer's exposure turns on the scope of employment, not on a civil versus criminal split.

ww.Allowed with a thirty-day notice: A notice period does not let a landlord keep a deposit for normal wear and tear; deductions are limited to unpaid rent and damage beyond ordinary use.
ww.Required to cover repainting costs: No state requires tenants to pay for repainting after normal wear; faded paint is ordinary use that the landlord absorbs as a cost of business.

map.The view that laws never change from yea: The view that ethics are fixed by the laws of each country
map.The belief in one set of ethical rules t: The view that the best action is the one with the best results

ww.The view that ethics are fixed by the la: That is closer to legal positivism; ethical relativism says right and wrong depend on cultural or personal standards rather than on written law.
ww.The view that the best action is the one: That describes consequentialism, which judges actions by outcomes; relativism instead holds that moral standards vary with culture or the individual.

ww.The Sherman Antitrust Act: The Sherman Act deals with monopolies and price fixing, not bribery of foreign officials, which is covered by the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act.
ww.The Truth in Lending Act: The Truth in Lending Act covers credit disclosures to consumers, not bribery of foreign officials by a U.S. company.

map.Doing what benefits oneself only, and ig: Judging actions by whether the person acting had good intentions
map.Following rules regardless of results, s: Following duties and rules no matter what the consequences are

ww.Judging actions by whether the person ac: Judging by intentions is closer to intent-based ethics; utilitarianism judges actions by their results for everyone affected.
ww.Following duties and rules no matter wha: That describes deontology, which focuses on duties; utilitarianism looks at outcomes and chooses the action producing the greatest overall good.

map.Judging only by results and the outcomes: Judging actions by the greatest good for the greatest number
map.Doing what is legal only, never the duti: Judging actions by the character of the person who acts

ww.Judging actions by the greatest good for: That describes utilitarianism, which weighs outcomes; deontology judges an act by whether it follows moral duties or rules.
ww.Judging actions by the character of the: That describes virtue ethics, which focuses on character; deontology judges the act itself by moral duties and rules.

map.Unlimited vacation for all workers, with: Paid sick leave for employees who miss work because of a long illness
map.Pay raises each year for every worker, s: Retirement accounts that employers must match with deposits from company funds each pay period

ww.Paid sick leave for employees who miss w: COBRA is about keeping group health insurance after job loss, not paid sick leave, which employers or other laws provide separately.
ww.Retirement accounts that employers must: Retirement account matching is not part of COBRA, which only lets former employees continue group health coverage by paying the premium.

map.Only the employee's wishes and what they: Company policy, since drug testing is treated as a private business matter
map.No rules at all, since each employer may: A federal law that requires employers to test new hires each year

ww.Company policy, since drug testing is tr: Company policy alone cannot decide testing; state and federal law, the nature of the job, and consent or notice set the limits on employers.
ww.A federal law that requires employers to: No general federal law requires employers to test new hires annually; testing is governed by various laws and depends on the job and notice.

map.Tips go to the employer, who may keep th: Employers pay the full minimum wage in cash and may keep a share of tips
map.Tips replace all wages, so the employer: Employers may pay a lower cash wage even if tips leave the worker below minimum wage

ww.Employers pay the full minimum wage in c: Employers may not keep employees' tips; the tip credit lets them pay a lower cash wage, not the full wage plus a share of tips.
ww.Employers may pay a lower cash wage even: If tips do not bring the worker up to the minimum wage, the employer must make up the difference, so the cash wage cannot leave the worker below it.

map.Banks to publish customer balances on a: Banks to freeze accounts of customers who owe back taxes
map.Banks to raise rates on loans for all of: Banks to hold a minimum reserve of customer deposits
map.Banks to avoid cash and take only electr: Banks to disclose loan costs and finance charges to borrowers

ww.Banks to freeze accounts of customers wh: Freezing accounts for tax debts is done through levies and legal process; the Act focuses on recordkeeping and reports to the government.
ww.Banks to hold a minimum reserve of custo: Reserve requirements are set by the Federal Reserve, while the Secrecy Act is an anti-money laundering law about reports and records.
ww.Banks to disclose loan costs and finance: Loan cost disclosure falls under the Truth in Lending Act; this Act requires reports on large cash transactions and suspicious activity.

map.They are identical in every respect and: A W-2 reports interest earned at a bank while a 1099 reports wages
map.A W-2 is only for businesses that file r: A W-2 is filed by the worker while a 1099 is filed by the employer

ww.A W-2 reports interest earned at a bank: A W-2 reports wages paid to employees, so it is not about bank interest, and a 1099 reports contractor payments rather than wages.
ww.A W-2 is filed by the worker while a 109: The employer files and issues the W-2 for wages; the worker does not file it, and a 1099 is issued to contractors by the payer.

map.Profits are never shared with any partne: Ownership can be sold freely on a stock market
map.There is only one decision maker in the: Decisions require approval from a board of directors

ww.Ownership can be sold freely on a stock: Partnership interests are not traded on stock markets; shares of corporations are, so this feature belongs to public corporations instead.
ww.Decisions require approval from a board: A board of directors is a corporate structure; partners usually make decisions together under their agreement, with no board required.

map.As costs rise, producers always make mor: As income rises, quantity supplied rises
map.As demand falls, prices always rise: As price rises, quantity demanded rises

ww.As income rises, quantity supplied rises: Rising income affects demand rather than supply; the law of supply links the price of a good to the quantity producers offer.
ww.As price rises, quantity demanded rises: That reverses the law of demand, which says quantity demanded falls as price rises; the law of supply concerns sellers, not buyers.

map.A product that is only sold by one compa: A product that buyers purchase more of as income rises
map.A product that has no price at all attac: A product made from the leftover materials of another

ww.A product that buyers purchase more of a: That describes a normal good, defined by how demand responds to income; a substitute is defined by replacing another product.
ww.A product made from the leftover materia: That describes a by-product of production; a substitute good is something buyers switch to when the price of another good changes.

map.A product that is sold only abroad and n: A product bought more often when income falls
map.A product that is given away for free to: A product sold by a company with no rivals

ww.A product bought more often when income: That describes an inferior good, defined by how demand responds to income; complements are goods used together, like cars and gasoline.
ww.A product sold by a company with no riva: That describes a monopoly product; complements are defined by being used together, so demand for one moves with demand for the other.

map.Prices always fall as consumption rises,: Prices fall as more units are produced by firms
map.Total satisfaction always falls with eac: Total satisfaction stops growing after the first unit

ww.Prices fall as more units are produced b: Diminishing marginal utility concerns the satisfaction a consumer gets, not firms' production or prices; it says each extra unit adds less satisfaction.
ww.Total satisfaction stops growing after t: Total satisfaction usually keeps rising as more is consumed, just at a slower rate; it does not stop growing after the first unit.

map.They have no economic value in the marke: They are taxed at a different rate than final goods
map.Intermediate goods are always illegal to: Their value is too small to measure accurately
map.They are produced abroad and never count: They are made by the government rather than by firms

ww.They are taxed at a different rate than: Tax rates are unrelated to the GDP rule; intermediate goods are left out because their value is already included in the price of final goods.
ww.Their value is too small to measure accu: Intermediate goods are large parts of economic activity and are measured; they are excluded to avoid double counting, not because they are small.
ww.They are made by the government rather t: Most intermediate goods are made by private firms; they are left out because their value is already counted in final goods, not because of who makes them.

map.Making every product in one workshop so: Producing a wide range of goods to avoid depending on trade
map.Buying goods only from foreign suppliers: Paying workers by the hour instead of by the piece

ww.Producing a wide range of goods to avoid: Producing many goods to avoid trade is self-sufficiency, the reverse of specialization, which concentrates effort on a few goods and relies on trade.
ww.Paying workers by the hour instead of by: The method of paying workers is unrelated to specialization, which refers to concentrating on a limited range of goods or tasks.

map.To make goods hard to trade at all: To lower the prices of goods
map.To ensure prices never change at all: To fix the amount banks may lend

ww.To lower the prices of goods: Money does not lower prices; prices are set by supply and demand, and money's role as a medium of exchange is to make trading easier.
ww.To fix the amount banks may lend: Limits on bank lending are set by regulators and reserve rules; money as a medium of exchange is simply what people accept in trade.

map.An economy in which only exports are all: An economy in which private owners compete freely for profit
map.An economy in which computers make all o: An economy in which government and private firms share decisions
map.An economy in which a central office set: An economy in which a central planner directs the output of firms

ww.An economy in which private owners compe: That describes a market economy, where private owners and competition guide decisions; a traditional economy relies on custom and habit.
ww.An economy in which government and priva: That describes a mixed economy; a traditional economy relies on customs handed down over generations.
ww.An economy in which a central planner di: That describes a command economy; in a traditional economy, customs and habits, not planners, guide what is produced and traded.

map.An economy based only on bartering goods: Government planning of prices and output
map.An economy with no private firms at all: Custom and habit guiding production decisions

ww.Government planning of prices and output: That describes a command economy; a mixed economy combines private choice with some government involvement rather than full planning.
ww.Private choice without government involv: That describes a pure market economy; a mixed economy includes some government involvement such as regulation and public services.
ww.Custom and habit guiding production deci: That describes a traditional economy; a mixed economy blends private choice with government involvement in the market.

map.A system in which people trade only by c: The government plans output for each industry
map.A system in which prices are set by law: Workers jointly own the factories and land

ww.The government plans output for each ind: That describes a command economy; capitalism relies on private owners and markets instead of government planning of output.
ww.Workers jointly own the factories and la: That describes collective ownership found in socialist or communal systems; capitalism relies on private ownership of the means of production.

map.It guarantees that every business will s: It sets the wages that workers earn in the market
map.It is banned by law for all firms in eve: It limits how much a firm may charge customers

ww.It sets the wages that workers earn in t: Wages come from labor supply and demand, not from profit; profit is the reward and signal for producers.
ww.It limits how much a firm may charge cus: Profit does not cap prices; in a market economy, firms set prices and profit is the reward that guides where resources go.

map.A single planner setting every price: Government ownership of the main industries
map.A ban on private businesses of any kind: Output decided by tradition and custom

ww.Government ownership of the main industr: That is a feature of socialist or command systems; a market economy relies on private firms competing for customers.
ww.Output decided by tradition and custom: That is a feature of a traditional economy; in a market economy, buyers and sellers decide what is produced.

map.A system in which no one may earn a prof: The government sets prices for major goods
map.A system in which every product is free: Firms must share profits with the state

ww.The government sets prices for major goo: Price setting by government is a feature of command economies; free enterprise lets businesses decide their own prices.
ww.Firms must share profits with the state: Sharing profits with the state is not part of free enterprise, where businesses keep their profits after paying taxes.

map.A cost that is paid only when a product: The extra cost of making one more unit of output
map.A cost that rises with every unit produc: A cost that changes with the amount of materials used

ww.The extra cost of making one more unit o: That describes marginal cost, which is the added cost of one more unit; a fixed cost does not change when output changes.
ww.A cost that changes with the amount of m: That describes a variable cost, which changes with output; a fixed cost stays the same whatever the amount produced.

map.A cost that is paid only once at start-u: A one-time charge paid to open the business
map.A cost that stays the same at all output: A cost that stays constant as output rises

ww.A one-time charge paid to open the busin: A one-time start-up charge does not change with output, so it behaves like a fixed cost rather than a variable cost.
ww.A cost that stays constant as output ris: A cost that stays constant as output rises is a fixed cost; a variable cost changes with the quantity produced.

map.Adding more inputs always increases outp: Output doubles when all inputs are doubled
map.Adding more inputs always reduces output: Total output falls as soon as a second worker is hired

ww.Output doubles when all inputs are doubl: That describes constant returns to scale; diminishing returns concern adding more of one input while others stay fixed.
ww.Total output falls as soon as a second w: Diminishing returns mean extra output shrinks over time, not that total output drops right after the second worker; early workers usually add more.

map.The owner is never liable for the busine: Shareholders lose just the money they invested
map.The business may never borrow money from: The firm cannot be sued by its customers

ww.Shareholders lose just the money they in: That describes limited liability, where owners risk only their investment; unlimited liability makes the owner personally responsible for business debts.
ww.The firm cannot be sued by its customers: Unlimited liability does not stop customers from suing; it means the owner's personal assets can be used to pay business debts.

map.A market with no sellers at all in it: A market with many sellers of identical goods
map.A market with only one seller present: A market with one buyer and many sellers

ww.A market with many sellers of identical: That describes perfect competition, where many small sellers offer the same product; an oligopoly has just a few large sellers.
ww.A market with one buyer and many sellers: That describes a monopsony, where one buyer dominates; an oligopoly is dominated by a few large sellers.

map.It guarantees much higher profits: It lifts a firm's after-tax earnings
map.It always increases hiring and pay: It raises the money available for expansion

ww.It lifts a firm's after-tax earnings: Higher taxes reduce after-tax earnings rather than lifting them, leaving the firm less to invest and hire.
ww.It raises the money available for expans: Higher taxes reduce the money a firm keeps, so there is less available for expansion, not more.

map.It is set by private firms only, not the: It is set separately by each employer
map.It always lowers inflation, so none disa: It is agreed to be harmless by most economists

ww.It is set separately by each employer: The minimum wage is set by law, federal or state, so employers cannot each set it themselves; economists debate its effects on jobs and incomes.
ww.It is agreed to be harmless by most econ: Economists do not agree it is harmless; some studies find job losses for certain workers, which is why the topic is debated.

ww.Adults who hold full-time jobs: The labor force includes part-time workers and job seekers too, so limiting it to full-time jobholders is too narrow.
ww.People who receive unemployment benefits: Many unemployed people do not receive benefits, and the labor force also includes all employed workers, so this definition is incomplete.

map.Income earned only from stock investment: Income earned from interest and dividends each year
map.Income spent on necessities only each mo: Income left after paying for housing and food

ww.Income earned from interest and dividend: That describes investment income, a source of earnings; disposable income is defined by taxes already being subtracted.
ww.Income left after paying for housing and: Disposable income is measured after taxes, and it may be spent or saved on anything; it is not defined by necessities.

map.Zero, because demand never responds to i: Zero, because demand stays flat as income rises
map.Infinite, because every buyer spends all: Equal to price elasticity, since both measure demand

ww.Zero, because demand stays flat as incom: Flat demand as income rises describes a good with zero income elasticity, not a normal good, whose demand increases with income.
ww.Equal to price elasticity, since both me: Income elasticity measures response to income and price elasticity measures response to price; they differ, and for a normal good income elasticity is positive.

map.Zero unemployment at all times in every: The rate when all workers hold a job in the economy
map.The rate set by law and fixed in every s: The rate that the central bank targets for each year

ww.The rate when all workers hold a job in: Zero unemployment does not occur even at full employment, because frictional and structural unemployment always exist.
ww.The rate that the central bank targets f: Central banks do not target the natural rate; it results from labor market conditions, mainly frictional and structural unemployment.

map.Incomes are always equal for all people: Wealth is shared equally among citizens

ww.Wealth is shared equally among citizens: Markets reward skills and ownership, so wealth is not shared equally; unequal outcomes are a known drawback of markets.
ww.Prices are set by officials: Officials set prices in command economies; in a market economy, prices come from the interaction of buyers and sellers.

map.A monopolist must charge the market pric: A monopolist faces the market price like rivals
map.A monopolist produces at zero profit in: A monopolist earns normal profit in the long run

ww.A monopolist faces the market price like: Competitive firms take the market price as given, but a monopolist has market power and picks its own price.
ww.A monopolist earns normal profit in the: Barriers to entry let a monopolist keep economic profit in the long run, unlike competitive firms whose profit is competed away.

map.A product that is always unprofitable fo: A product that stores sell at the highest markup
map.A product given away for free forever to: A product priced high to signal quality

ww.A product that stores sell at the highes: A loss leader is priced low on purpose to draw shoppers, not priced high; it is the opposite of a high-markup product.
ww.A product priced high to signal quality: Pricing high to signal quality is prestige pricing; a loss leader is priced low to attract customers who buy other items.

map.A period when every input can be changed: A period when firms can change plant size
map.A period lasting exactly one month in to: A period shorter than one calendar year

ww.A period when firms can change plant siz: That describes the long run, when all inputs including plant size can change; in the short run at least one input is fixed.
ww.A period shorter than one calendar year: The short run is defined by fixed inputs, not by calendar time; its length differs across industries.

map.Prices rise without any limit at all: Existing firms raise prices to raise profit

ww.Existing firms raise prices to raise pro: Competitive firms are price takers and cannot raise prices; economic profit draws in new firms, which lowers price.
ww.The government takes the profit: Governments do not take profit away in a competitive industry; entry by new firms is what reduces profit over time.

map.A corporation that never pays tax to any: A corporation taxed twice on its profits
map.A corporation formed only abroad in a fo: A corporation formed to serve charities

ww.A corporation taxed twice on its profits: Double taxation describes a C corporation; an S corporation passes income to its owners to avoid taxation at the corporate level.
ww.A corporation formed to serve charities: A corporation formed for charity is a nonprofit; an S corporation is a for-profit firm with a special pass-through tax status.

map.Only the owners of the business itself: Owners who invest money in the firm
map.Only the managers of the business itself: Managers who run the daily work

ww.Owners who invest money in the firm: Owners are one stakeholder group, but stakeholders include anyone affected by the firm, so this is too narrow.
ww.Rivals that sell similar goods: Rivals can be affected, but stakeholders also include employees, customers, suppliers and communities.
ww.Managers who run the daily work: Managers are stakeholders, but the term is wider and includes anyone affected by or with an interest in the firm.

map.Spending has no effect on income or outp: Spending raises output by just the amount that was spent
map.Spending always lowers output in the eco: Spending crowds out private spending by the same amount

ww.Spending raises output by just the amoun: The multiplier means output rises by more than the original spending, because recipients re-spend part of what they receive.
ww.Spending crowds out private spending by: Full crowding out is an extreme view; the multiplier effect says spending is re-spent and raises output by more than the first round.

map.A statistic that tends to change only af: A statistic that tends to change after the economy does
map.A statistic that never changes over any: A statistic that moves at the same time as the economy

ww.A statistic that tends to change after t: That describes a lagging indicator, such as the unemployment rate; a leading indicator changes before the economy turns.
ww.A statistic that moves at the same time: That describes a coincident indicator, such as industrial production; a leading indicator changes ahead of the economy.

map.One country gains only at another's expe: Countries gain by selling more than they buy from abroad
map.All countries must make every good they: Countries gain by making the goods that they use most
map.Trade removes the need for specializatio: Countries gain by taxing imports to shield domestic firms from rivals

ww.Countries gain by selling more than they: That is the mercantilist view; comparative advantage shows trade benefits both sides, even when imports exceed exports.
ww.Countries gain by making the goods that: Making the goods they use most ignores opportunity cost; gains come from producing what a country makes at lower opportunity cost.
ww.Countries gain by taxing imports to shie: Import taxes shield local firms but reduce the gains from trade; comparative advantage relies on specializing and trading freely.

map.Only a tool for taxes and fees paid by t: Means of production, unit of account and store of debt
map.Only a way to decorate a wallet, with li: Source of income, unit of trade and store of labor
map.Only a measure of weight for goods, gold: Medium of exchange, measure of supply and source of credit

ww.Means of production, unit of account and: Money is not a means of production, and it stores value rather than debt; its functions are medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value.
ww.Source of income, unit of trade and stor: Money does not store labor, and source of income is not a standard function; the three functions are exchange, account and value storage.
ww.Medium of exchange, measure of supply an: Measure of supply and source of credit are not standard functions of money; the third function is storing value, not supplying credit.

map.The ability to charge more than all of t: The ability to sell goods in more foreign markets
map.The ability to ban imports from all of t: The ability to impose tariffs on goods from foreign firms

ww.The ability to sell goods in more foreig: Selling in more markets reflects market reach, not opportunity cost; comparative advantage concerns what a producer gives up to make a good.
ww.The ability to impose tariffs on goods f: Tariffs are a policy tool of governments, not an ability to produce; comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost.

map.Only government workers and public emplo: Adults who are employed or in school
map.Only people with full-time jobs, not par: People who are unemployed and collecting benefits

ww.Adults who are employed or in school: Students who are not working or looking for work are outside the labor force; it counts only workers and job seekers.
ww.People who are unemployed and collecting: The labor force includes the employed as well as job seekers, so restricting it to people collecting benefits leaves out most workers.

map.There are no sellers at all in any singl: Firms face barriers to entry in monopolistic competition
map.There is only one seller in the whole ma: Firms are price takers in monopolistic competition

ww.Firms face barriers to entry in monopoli: Monopolistic competition has few barriers to entry, so new firms can join; the key difference from perfect competition is differentiated products.
ww.Firms are price takers in monopolistic c: Firms with differentiated products have some control over price, unlike price takers in perfect competition.

map.The assumption that people always give t: The assumption that people choose whatever their neighbors expect of them
map.The assumption that people never trade,: The assumption that people ignore costs and prices when they decide

ww.The assumption that people choose whatev: Rational self-interest assumes people weigh costs and benefits for themselves; it does not assume they follow their neighbors' expectations.
ww.The assumption that people ignore costs: Rational choice assumes people weigh costs and prices carefully; ignoring them would be irrational behavior.

map.Rent only, since rent is fixed always: Rent, because leases last for several years
map.Wages only, since wages are fixed: Wages, because workers sign long-term contracts

ww.Rent, because leases last for several ye: In the long run a firm can move or renegotiate its lease, so rent can be changed and is not fixed.
ww.Wages, because workers sign long-term co: Contracts end or can be renegotiated over time, so in the long run wages can be changed and are not fixed.

map.Never shut down, whatever the price or t: Shut down if price is below average fixed cost
map.Shut down every winter for a few months: Shut down if the firm is losing money

ww.Shut down if price is below average fixe: Fixed costs must be paid whether or not the firm produces, so they do not drive the shutdown decision; the test is average variable cost.
ww.Shut down if the firm is losing money: A firm losing money may still cover variable costs and part of fixed costs by producing, so it should keep running while price exceeds average variable cost.

map.Lower taxes always lower revenue, since: Tax revenue rises in proportion to the tax rate at high levels
map.Taxes never affect behavior at all, whet: Tax rates matter less than the size of government spending
map.Taxes always raise more revenue as rates: Revenue is highest when the tax rate reaches one hundred percent

ww.Tax revenue rises in proportion to the t: The Laffer curve says revenue stops rising at high rates and then falls, so revenue does not keep increasing in proportion to the rate.
ww.Tax rates matter less than the size of g: The Laffer curve is about how tax rates change behavior and revenue, not about government spending.
ww.Revenue is highest when the tax rate rea: At a rate of one hundred percent, people would stop reporting taxable income, so revenue would fall; the peak is at a lower rate.

map.Firms with no factories and no fixed cos: Foreign firms that sell the same goods in other countries
map.Customers only, who pay a higher price f: Firms that already installed the pollution controls last year

ww.Foreign firms that sell the same goods i: Foreign firms selling abroad are not covered by this domestic factory rule, so they face no new cost from it.
ww.Firms that already installed the polluti: Firms that already installed controls have paid the cost and do not face the new burden, so they are not hurt most.

map.Excess competition between firms that le: Firms compete so heavily that prices fall below production costs
map.Too many choices for consumers in every: Consumers face a flood of products and brands to choose from

ww.Firms compete so heavily that prices fal: Central planning replaces competition among firms, so price wars are not its drawback; its problem is that planners lack information.
ww.Consumers face a flood of products and b: Central planning usually limits consumer choice and causes shortages, so an overload of choices is not its drawback.

map.A system with no taxes of any kind, whet: A system with rule by one party and no private ownership of property
map.A system with no markets at all, in whic: A system in which a king or military ruler controls the economy

ww.A system with rule by one party and no p: That describes a one-party communist system; democratic socialism keeps free elections and allows private property alongside public programs.
ww.A system in which a king or military rul: That describes authoritarian rule; democratic socialism keeps elected government and a mixed economy.

map.Lowering all costs of making goods and s: Replacing higher-cost domestic production with cheaper imports from a partner inside the union
map.Banning all trade between the member cou: Raising tariffs on goods traded between member countries to protect local producers

ww.Replacing higher-cost domestic productio: That describes trade creation, which improves efficiency; trade diversion shifts imports from a cheaper outside country to a costlier member.
ww.Raising tariffs on goods traded between: A customs union removes tariffs among members; trade diversion happens because of the common external tariff against outsiders.

map.Setting wages for workers by using the s: Measuring how unevenly income is divided across households in a nation
map.Measuring GDP by adding up the output of: Calculating the average price of a basket of consumer goods

ww.Measuring how unevenly income is divided: That describes inequality measures such as the Gini index; the poverty line is an income threshold for basic needs.
ww.Calculating the average price of a baske: That describes the consumer price index; the poverty line is an income threshold used to identify households in poverty.

map.They never change at all in value: They stay fixed until bonds mature

ww.They stay fixed until bonds mature: Bond prices change daily in the market; they respond to interest rate changes rather than staying fixed until maturity.
ww.They rise and fall together: When interest rates rise, existing bonds with lower payments lose value, so the two move in opposite directions.

map.The view that prices never change over t: The view that government spending is the main driver of inflation and output in the short run
map.The view that trade is useless and that: The view that wages set by unions are the main driver of inflation in the economy

ww.The view that government spending is the: That describes a Keynesian-style view; monetarism holds that changes in the money supply are the main driver of inflation and output.
ww.The view that wages set by unions are th: Monetarists see inflation as caused by money supply growth rather than union wages, so this does not describe monetarism.

map.The debt is yearly only, and the deficit: The debt is foreign borrowing while the deficit is borrowing from citizens
map.The deficit is the total owed while the: The deficit measures spending while the debt measures tax collected

ww.The debt is foreign borrowing while the: The debt is the total of all past borrowing from any lender, and the deficit is the yearly shortfall; neither is defined by who lends.
ww.The deficit measures spending while the: The deficit is the yearly gap when spending exceeds revenue, and the debt is the total owed from past borrowing, not tax collected.

map.Looking at the past only, and never at t: Comparing the average cost of an action with its average price
map.Ignoring costs and benefits when making: Choosing the option that has the lowest total cost of production
map.Comparing total costs only, with no look: Comparing the total benefit of an action with its total cost

ww.Comparing the average cost of an action: Marginal analysis looks at the extra benefit and extra cost of one more unit, not at averages.
ww.Choosing the option that has the lowest: Choosing the lowest total cost ignores benefits; marginal analysis weighs the extra benefit against the extra cost.
ww.Comparing the total benefit of an action: That is total analysis; marginal analysis compares only the added benefit and added cost of one more unit.

map.Zero profit always, whatever the market: The ability to raise price because many rivals sell the same product
map.A legal price cap imposed by the governm: The ability to cut price below marginal cost to attract more buyers

ww.The ability to raise price because many: Many rivals selling the same product describes competition, which limits price; a monopoly has pricing power because it has no close substitutes.
ww.The ability to cut price below marginal: A monopolist maximizes profit by pricing above marginal cost, not below it; cutting below marginal cost would lose money on each unit.

map.Money loses value only on weekends and p: A dollar in the future is worth more than a dollar today
map.Interest rates never change in any count: Interest earned on savings is taxed at the same rate as wages
map.A dollar is worth the same at any time,: Money keeps its value best when it is held as cash

ww.A dollar in the future is worth more tha: That reverses the concept; a dollar today can earn interest, so it is worth more than the same dollar received later.
ww.Interest earned on savings is taxed at t: Tax treatment of interest is unrelated to the time value of money, which says money today is worth more than money later.
ww.Money keeps its value best when it is he: Cash loses buying power through inflation and earns no interest, which is why money today can be worth more when invested.

map.Investing only in cash and savings: Borrowing money to buy more stock
map.Putting all of the money in one stock: Timing the market to buy low

ww.Borrowing money to buy more stock: Borrowing to buy stock is leverage and increases risk; diversification spreads investments across assets to reduce risk.
ww.Timing the market to buy low: Timing the market is an attempt to predict prices and does not spread risk; diversification holds many different investments.
